column2: On the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “There are four [traits]: whoever has them is a hypocrite,

and whoever has one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he gives it up: when he speaks, he lies; when he makes a promise, he breaks it; when he disputes, he transgresses; and when he makes a covenant, he betrays it.” Agreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim).
Arbaʿ (“four”): traits. “A pure hypocrite”: [in] hypocrisy of action.
Minhunna (“of them”): of these four.
Khaṣlah, with fatḥah on the khāʾ: a characteristic. Yadaʿahā (“he gives it up”): he leaves it. Ḥaddatha (“he speaks”): he reports.
Kadhaba (“he lies”): to pave the way for his excuse and aim, so that he is not blamed for some shortcoming, or for some other purpose.
“When he makes a promise, he breaks it”: he does not keep his promise.
Fajara (“he transgresses”): he deviates from the truth in the dispute.
Ghadara (“he betrays it”): he breaks the covenant.
A warning against taking on these traits, which consist of showing what is right while concealing, in reality, what contradicts it.
Leaving these traits is part of the soundness of society, and committing them part of its corruption and disorder.
Whoever has all these traits has complete hypocrisy of action.

Urging the reform of speech, action and intention; for among the corruptions of speech is lying, among the corruptions of intention is breaking promises, and among the corruptions of action is betraying covenants.

The noble Prophet ﷺ warns us against taking on these four traits, since some Muslims commit some of them; for whoever commits one has a branch of hypocrisy in him, and if he has all of them, he is a pure hypocrite.
So let the Muslims beware of taking on these corrupt traits, which corrupt both the individual and society;

among their effects is that trust is lost in whoever has these traits, and others imitate him until they spread among people, so that nothing goes right for them because they do not trust one another.

We, the company of Muslims, must therefore keep away from these traits and adopt fine manners and virtuous character, so that we are a good example to one another and to the new generation of our children.
You lied, and whoever lies, his recompense / when he brings the truth is not to be believed.
Once the liar is known for lying, he remains / a liar in people's eyes, even when he tells the truth.
Another poet:
If you say “yes” to something, fulfil it, / for “yes” is a debt binding on the free man.
Otherwise say “no”, and be at rest and give rest by it, / lest people say that you are a liar.
Another poet:
Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, / and no hand gives except from what it finds.
So make no promise unless you keep it, / and beware of going back on your word to the one you promise.
Another poet:
You promised, and you are the most generous of those who promise; / there is no good in a promise that is not fulfilled.
Another poet:
Keep faith with trusts and avoid treachery; / be just and do not wrong, and your gain will be good.
Another poet:
Betraying a covenant is exceedingly ugly; / the worst of mankind is one who does not keep a covenant.
But in this age of ours we are as the poet said:
Loyalty has dried up and treachery overflowed, / and the gap of discord has widened between word and deed.
